resumen: Holding a kettlebell with both hands, you hike it back between your legs with a hip hinge and drive it forward to chest height with a snap of the hips. An explosive exercise for the glutes and hamstrings.
ejecucion: Stand with your feet slightly wider than your hips and the kettlebell on the floor, a hand’s length in front of your feet.
With a straight back, push your hips back, grip the handle with both hands and hike it back between your legs, like a football snap: the bell travels high, close to the groin, not down by the knees.
Drive your hips forward hard, squeezing your glutes, so the kettlebell swings forward on straight arms up to chest height. Your arms do not lift it: they only guide it.
At the top, stand tall as in a plank, abs and glutes tight, without leaning back or arching your lower back.
Let it fall and, when your forearms touch your thighs, push your hips back again for the next swing.
When you finish, let it lose momentum and set it on the floor in front of you with a straight back.
If your back rounds at the bottom or you are pulling with your arms, lower the weight or practise the kettlebell deadlift first.
matices: In a study of seven men with a 16 kg kettlebell, the swing took the glutes to 80 % of their maximal contraction and the low back extensors to 50 %, in rapid pulses of activation and relaxation, with about 3,200 N of low back compression. The authors note that many credit it with improving their back, but a few find it irritating. Another study, in twenty-three people, found that the biceps femoris reaches peak activation before the glutes, and a moderate correlation between hip flexor length and gluteus maximus activation.
